title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 14: Invest in the Whole Country, Not Just in the Mining Industry
keywords: La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos
full control and supervision of the State
rule of law -- not of men
Department of Environment and Natural Resources
primary_topics: Chapter 14 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- the address CJP delivered to an international gathering of mining investors explaining, in lay terms, the Supreme Court's landmark Decision upholding the constitutionality of the Mining Law and defining the extent of foreign participation in large-scale mining.

A primer on the Philippine constitutional system for foreign investors: three coequal and coindependent branches that coordinate and check one another, and a judiciary uniquely mandated to nullify any governmental act tainted with grave abuse of discretion.

A ten-point outline of La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos: who may enter FTAAs, what resources they cover, the State's full control and supervision, the President's and DENR secretary's role, the contractor's reasonable prerogatives, and the President's discretion over the fiscal regime.

The Court's answer to environmental and social objections -- that priority for mining is a question of policy for the President and Congress, not of constitutionality -- coupled with a plea that investors take a longer view and invest in the whole country, not just the mining industry.
sub_topics: CJP frames the speech as a macro view of the legal system before turning to the mining Decision itself.
He describes a republican, presidential government whose three branches are coequal and coindependent, neither antagonistic nor subservient, coordinating and checking one another.
He stresses judicial independence and the constitutional mandate to strike down gravely abusive acts as a duty rather than a power -- a power can be relinquished, a duty cannot.
He lists what the Court has nullified on that ground: laws, executive orders, acts of cabinet secretaries, bureau directors and top military and police officers, and government contracts.
He defines grave abuse of discretion as acting contrary to the Constitution, law or jurisprudence, or whimsically and arbitrarily to the point of evading a positive duty.
He insists the Court is not superior to the President or Congress: in case of doubt it upholds legislative and executive acts, because the rule of law, not of men, prevails.
He assures investors that trampled legal or contractual rights have a final recourse to an independent and fair Supreme Court, and describes the adversarial system of adjudication.
He cites the constitutional recognition of the private sector, due process and equal protection for aliens, and Philippine adherence to free trade as a WTO signatory.

He explains why government contracts are sometimes voided -- contracts violating the Constitution or laws are void -- and advises investors to follow the rules honestly, engage credible counsel before contracting, and avoid bribery, referring them to his book Leveling the Playing Field.

He sets out the constitutional baseline: all minerals are owned by the State, and EDU is generally through co-production, joint venture or production-sharing agreements with entities at least 60 percent Filipino-owned.

He notes the exception for large-scale EDU through FTAAs with 100-percent foreign-owned companies, and that the Decision became final on February 1, 2005 when the Motion for Reconsideration was denied 10-4 with one abstention.

Points one to five: FTAAs may be entered only with the President; cover only minerals, petroleum and other mineral oils; remain subject to the State's full control and supervision; are administered by the President through the DENR secretary as alter ego; and must abide by RA 7942 and its rules.
He analogizes the State's full control to a corporate board that may delegate managerial and operational functions while retaining full residual control.

Points six to eight: FOCs bear all financial, technical and entrepreneurial risk and may be granted reasonable prerogatives to protect their investments, the President may specify terms including the fiscal regime, and the Court will not inordinately interfere absent grave abuse of discretion.
Point nine: the whole Court agreed the Constitution allows FTAAs; the dispute was over the extent of foreign participation and executive discretion over the government's share of financial benefits.
He summarizes the four dissenters' demand for a minimum 60 percent government share of net mining revenues and their claim that the law would leave the State only taxes and fees.

He quotes the Court's answer -- no constitutional authority to fix such a minimum -- and its overriding policy that the Constitution should be read in broad, life-giving strokes, adding that fairness is a credo in law and in business.

He notes the Court's caution to the Chief Executive to secure the best terms, and its warning that officials who agree to grossly disadvantageous shares will answer to the courts and the provision will be voided.
Point ten: the petitioners' argument from the OXFAM America Research Report and a World Bank report about mining-dependent communities, environmental degradation and uneven sharing of benefits.

He quotes the Court's reply that priority for mining is a question of policy for the President and Congress, since the Court declares what the Constitution and laws say and refrains from delving into policy.

He describes the Court's countervailing assurances: the State's residual control can demand best mining practices, protect indigenous rights and prevent degradation, and the Implementing Rules distribute benefits 50 percent national, 10 percent provincial, 20 percent municipal, 20 percent to affected barangays.

He acknowledges negative reactions rooted in the Marinduque Mining and Marcopper experience and denunciations by Catholic and non-Catholic religious groups, and the Court's call to prevent irreversible ecological damage.

He closes by noting the Decision's record 246 pages in the Court's 104-year history, its call for an appropriate balancing of interests and needs, and his plea that investors help develop the whole country and its people's prosperity.
signature_phrases: A power can be relinquished, but a duty cannot be evaded under any circumstance.
the rule of law -- not of men -- prevails
It should not be used to strangulate economic growth or to serve narrow, parochial interests

the entire Filipino nation, present and future, to whom the mineral wealth really belongs
large-scale mining ventures are really permanent investments in the long-term development of the whole country
invest not just in the mining industry. Invest in our country. Invest in our people's prosperity.

stances.claim: The constitutional mandate to nullify gravely abusive acts of any branch or official is a duty, not merely a power, and therefore cannot be evaded -- yet in exercising it the Court is not superior to the President or Congress but only makes the Constitution and laws reign supreme.
stances.rhetorical_move: duty-versus-power distinction followed immediately by a disclaimer of judicial supremacy, to reassure rather than alarm a foreign audience

stances.claim: The State's 'full control and supervision' over mineral resources is like a corporate board's: managerial, operational, financial and marketing functions may be delegated to the contractor while the State retains full residual control and the power to set aside, reverse or modify its plans.
stances.rhetorical_move: business analogy chosen for an audience of investors, quoting the Decision's own formulation

stances.claim: The Court could not fix a minimum 60 percent government share of net mining revenues because no constitutional provision empowers it to do so; the President must instead be given leeway to negotiate FTAAs.
stances.rhetorical_move: answering the dissent on the ground of judicial competence rather than of desirability, while conceding the Court favors maximum benefits for the people

stances.claim: Environmental, social and priority-setting objections to mining, however valid and important, are questions of policy for the President and Congress and lie outside the constitutional authority of the Court.
stances.rhetorical_move: jurisdictional deflection softened by listing the residual controls and benefit-sharing rules that do address those concerns

stances.claim: Investors should take a wider and longer-term view, because large-scale mining is in reality a permanent investment in the development of the whole country, and inequitable sharing or neglect of the environment would bring resentment and instability that harms investors too.
stances.rhetorical_move: appeal to the audience's self-interest as the bridge to a national appeal, closing on the triple imperative to invest in the country and the people's prosperity

notable_anecdotes: CJP notes that the Decision became final 'just the other day, February 1, 2005,' when the Court turned down the Motion for Reconsideration by the same 10-4 vote with one abstention.

He remarks that the Decision ran to 246 double-spaced legal-sized pages, the longest in the 104-year history of the Court, reflecting the extraordinary deliberations and the justices' effort to go beyond strictly legal parameters.

He recalls the negative public reactions to the ruling, owing largely to past experiences with local companies such as Marinduque Mining and Marcopper, and denunciations of mining by Catholic and non-Catholic religious groups.

He tells investors plainly how to protect their contracts: follow the rules honestly, engage credible lawyers before rather than after contracting, and avoid transactions that require bribing officials.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces Justice Panganiban's address to an international gathering of mining investors, delivered weeks after the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Mining Law. He began with a primer on the Philippine system: a republican, presidential government whose three branches are coequal and coindependent, coordinating and checking one another, and a judiciary constitutionally bound to nullify any act done with grave abuse of discretion -- a duty, he stressed, not merely a power, since a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot be evaded. He assured his audience that despite this authority the Court is not superior to the political branches, upholds their acts in case of doubt, and offers investors a final, independent recourse when their rights are trampled, adding practical advice to follow the rules honestly, hire credible counsel before contracting and avoid bribery. Turning to La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos, which had become final on February 1, 2005 when the Motion for Reconsideration was denied 10-4 with one abstention, he outlined ten features of the ruling: FTAAs may be entered only by the President and only with corporations; they cover only minerals, petroleum and other mineral oils; EDU remains under the State's full control and supervision, exercised through the President and the DENR secretary as alter ego; FTAAs must conform to RA 7942 and its rules; foreign-owned companies bear all the risk and may be granted reasonable managerial and marketing prerogatives while the State retains board-like residual control; the President may set the fiscal regime; and the Court will not inordinately interfere absent grave abuse. He explained that the entire Court agreed FTAAs were permissible and that the dispute concerned executive discretion over the government's share, rejecting the four dissenters' demand for a 60 percent minimum because no constitutional provision empowered the Court to fix it, and quoting the ruling that the Constitution should be read in broad, life-giving strokes. He then addressed the petitioners' OXFAM and World Bank evidence on mining-dependent communities and environmental degradation with the Court's answer that priority for mining is a policy question for the President and Congress, while noting the residual controls, the mandated distribution of benefits among national, provincial, municipal and barangay levels, and the exhortation to prevent irreversible ecological damage. He closed by citing the Decision's record 246 pages, its call for an appropriate balancing of interests and needs, and his own plea that investors help develop not just the mining industry but the whole country and its people's prosperity.
